# Fundamentals of Data Visualization {.divider}

[Chart design principles · Day 01]{.eyebrow}

<!-- slide 8 -->
## The Lie Factor {.smaller}

[Honest charts · baselines]{.eyebrow}

### Set bars to zero

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Bars encode by **length**, so the value axis must start at zero. Truncate it and a routine batch looks like one sample failed.

Lines and dots can be zoomed, just label the axis.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-dpi: 200
reads = load_reads_per_sample()                 # sample, reads (M)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 4.4))  # two panels side by side

# MISLEADING: y-axis starts at 30, so a small gap looks huge
ax[0].bar(reads["sample"], reads["reads"],
          color="#f4ab5c", edgecolor=CREAM)
ax[0].set_ylim(30, 42)                           # the lie: truncated baseline
ax[0].set_title("MISLEADING", color="#333333",
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[0].set_ylabel("reads per sample (M)")

# HONEST: y-axis starts at 0, so bar lengths are proportional
ax[1].bar(reads["sample"], reads["reads"],
          color="#d1422f", edgecolor=CREAM)
ax[1].set_ylim(0, 45)                            # honest: zero baseline
ax[1].set_title("HONEST", color="#333333",
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[1].axhline(0, color=INK, lw=1.5)              # anchor the eye at zero
for t in ax[1].get_yticklabels():               # make the 0 tick dark + bold
    if t.get_text() in ("0", "0.0"):
        t.set_color(INK); t.set_fontweight("bold")

for a in ax:                                     # tidy both panels
    a.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8)
    a.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.35, bottom=0.12)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 4.4))  # two panels side by side

# MISLEADING: y-axis starts at 30, so a small gap looks huge

          color="#f4ab5c", edgecolor=CREAM)
ax[0].set_ylim(30, 42)                           # the lie: truncated baseline
ax[0].set_title("MISLEADING", color="#333333",
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[0].set_ylabel("reads per sample (M)")

# HONEST: y-axis starts at 0, so bar lengths are proportional
ax[1].bar(reads["sample"], reads["reads"],
          color="#d1422f", edgecolor=CREAM)
ax[1].set_ylim(0, 45)                            # honest: zero baseline
ax[1].set_title("HONEST", color="#333333",
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[1].axhline(0, color=INK, lw=1.5)              # anchor the eye at zero
for t in ax[1].get_yticklabels():               # make the 0 tick dark + bold
    if t.get_text() in ("0", "0.0"):
        t.set_color(INK); t.set_fontweight("bold")

    a.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8)
    a.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
```

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Bars start at **zero**. Lines and dots can be zoomed, just label the axis.
:::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666;"}
After Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization* (2019), ch. 17.
:::

<!-- slide 9 -->
## Data-to-Ink Ratio {.smaller}

[Honest charts · simplicity]{.eyebrow}

### Remove what doesn't help, keep what does

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Every drop of ink should encode data. Strip the gridlines, hatching, and heavy borders, keep the bars and the numbers.

Like seasoning: too much overwhelms, too little is bland.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-dpi: 200
te = load_tissue_expression()          # tissue, tpm
ts = te.sort_values("tpm")             # sort so bars rank cleanly
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.6))

# TOO MUCH INK: grid + hatch + heavy borders all fight the data
ax[0].bar(te["tissue"], te["tpm"], color=PURPLE,
          edgecolor=INK, linewidth=1.5, hatch="//")
ax[0].grid(True, color=GREY)
ax[0].set_title("TOO MUCH INK", color=RED,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[0].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45, labelsize=7)

# JUST RIGHT: clean bars, value labels, no chartjunk
ax[1].barh(ts["tissue"], ts["tpm"],
           color=GREEN, height=0.62)
for i, v in enumerate(ts["tpm"]):      # label each bar with its value
    ax[1].text(v + 1, i, str(v), va="center",
               fontsize=9, color=MUTED)
ax[1].set_title("JUST RIGHT", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[1].set_xlim(0, 105)
for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:   # drop unneeded spines
    ax[1].spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax[1].xaxis.set_visible(False)         # values are labelled, axis is redundant
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.5, bottom=0.18)
plt.show()
```

### Code


:::

::: {.takeaway}
Maximise the share of ink that encodes real data. The right amount lets the data shine.

<!-- slide 10 -->
## Length Beats Area {.smaller}

[Honest charts · geometric accuracy]{.eyebrow}

### Compare with bars, not slices

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
The eye judges **length** well and **area** poorly. A pie asks you to compare wedge areas, and the small ancestry components blur together. The same proportions as bars rank in an instant.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-dpi: 200
adm = load_admixture()                 # individual, population, K1..K5
K = [f"K{i+1}" for i in range(5)]

# pick the most admixed individual (highest entropy = most mixed)
ent = -(adm[K].values
        * np.log(adm[K].values + 1e-9)).sum(1)
one = adm[K].iloc[ent.argmax()].values
cols = [BLUE, AMBER, GREEN, RED, PURPLE]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 4.7))

# PIE: wedge areas are hard to compare, tiny slices blur together
ax[0].pie(one, labels=K, colors=cols,
          autopct="%1.0f%%", startangle=90,
          textprops={"fontsize": 8})
ax[0].set_title("PIE: HARD", color=RED,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)

# BAR: sort, then rank by length, the eye reads it instantly
order = np.argsort(one)
ax[1].barh(np.array(K)[order], one[order] * 100,
           color=np.array(cols)[order], height=0.6)
for i, v in enumerate(one[order] * 100):
    ax[1].text(v + 1, i, f"{v:.0f}%", va="center",
               fontsize=9, color=MUTED)
ax[1].set_title("BAR: EASY", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[1].set_xlim(0, one.max() * 100 + 12)
for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
    ax[1].spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax[1].xaxis.set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.5)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 11 -->
## How We See: Perceptual Ranking {.smaller}

[Honest charts · perception]{.eyebrow}

### Position is read most accurately, colour least

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="42%"}
The same four values, four ways. Position is read most accurately, then length, then area, and colour least of all.

Encode your **main message** with position or length, reserve area and colour for secondary variables.
::::

:::: {.column width="58%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-dpi: 200
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 5))
labels = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
vals = [75, 50, 90, 30]                # same values, four encodings

# 1. POSITION on a common scale, read most accurately
ax[0, 0].scatter(vals, range(4), color=GREEN,
                 s=90, zorder=3)
ax[0, 0].set_yticks(range(4))
ax[0, 0].set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=8)
ax[0, 0].set_xlim(0, 100)
ax[0, 0].set_title("1. POSITION", color="#333333",
                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# 2. LENGTH of a bar, next most accurate
ax[0, 1].barh(labels, vals, color=BLUE, height=0.55)
ax[0, 1].set_xlim(0, 100)
ax[0, 1].set_title("2. LENGTH", color="#333333",
                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# 3. AREA of a bubble (s = size), harder to judge
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax[1, 0].scatter(i, 0.5, s=v * 8, color=PURPLE,
                     alpha=0.75, edgecolors=CREAM)
    ax[1, 0].text(i, -0.15, labels[i], ha="center",
                  fontsize=8, color=MUTED)
ax[1, 0].set_ylim(-0.5, 1.2)
ax[1, 0].set_xlim(-0.8, 3.8)
ax[1, 0].axis("off")
ax[1, 0].set_title("3. AREA", color="#333333",
                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# 4. COLOUR shade, read least accurately of all
cmap = econ_cmap("hongkong", reverse=True)
norm = plt.Normalize(0, 100)
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax[1, 1].barh(labels[i], 1, color=cmap(norm(v)),
                  height=0.6)
    ax[1, 1].text(0.5, i, str(v), ha="center",
                  va="center", fontsize=9,
                  fontweight="bold",
                  color=CREAM if v > 55 else INK)
ax[1, 1].set_xlim(0, 1)
ax[1, 1].xaxis.set_visible(False)
for s in ax[1, 1].spines.values():
    s.set_visible(False)
ax[1, 1].set_title("4. COLOUR", color="#333333",
                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.35, hspace=0.45)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 12 -->
## Pre-attentive Pop-out {.smaller}

[Honest charts · perception]{.eyebrow}

### Find the hit: a slow hunt, or an instant pop

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Same Manhattan plot, same significant SNP. On the left every point is grey, so you have to **hunt** along the line for the hit. On the right one highlight colour makes it **pop out** before you even look.

Colour, size, and orientation are pre-attentive. Encode the thing you want seen first with one of them.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-dpi: 200
g = load_gwas().copy()                 # chrom, pos, pval (SNP-level)
g["nlp"] = -np.log10(g["pval"])
g["i"] = range(len(g))                 # simple running x position
gw = -np.log10(5e-8)                    # genome-wide significance line
sig = g["nlp"] > gw

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.6, 3.4))

# ALL GREY: the hit is there, but you must hunt for it
ax[0].scatter(g["i"], g["nlp"], c=GREY, s=7, edgecolors="none")
ax[0].axhline(gw, color=GREY, lw=0.8, ls="--")
ax[0].set_title("ALL GREY: HUNT FOR IT", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[0].set_ylabel("-log10 p", fontsize=8)

# ONE COLOUR: highlight the significant SNP, it pops out
ax[1].scatter(g["i"][~sig], g["nlp"][~sig], c=GREY, s=7, edgecolors="none")
ax[1].scatter(g["i"][sig], g["nlp"][sig], c=RED, s=40,
              edgecolors=CREAM, lw=0.5, zorder=5)
ax[1].axhline(gw, color=GREY, lw=0.8, ls="--")
ax[1].set_title("ONE COLOUR: POPS OUT", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)

for a in ax:
    a.set_xticks([]); a.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    a.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.2, bottom=0.12)
plt.show()
```

### Code


<!-- slide 12.1 -->
## Pre-attentive: Size {.smaller}

[Honest charts · perception]{.eyebrow}

### Make the size mean something, hubs jump out

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
In a co-expression network, every gene drawn the same size hides the structure. Map node **size to the number of connections** and the hub genes pop out instantly, no labels, no hunting.

Size is pre-attentive: bigger reads as "more" before you think.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 3.6
import networkx as nx
G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(40, 2, seed=7)   # scale-free: a few hubs
deg = dict(G.degree())                         # connections per node
pos = nx.spring_layout(G, seed=7, k=0.5)
sizes = np.array([deg[n] for n in G.nodes()])
hub = max(deg.values())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.6, 3.6))
for a in ax:
    a.axis("off")

# UNIFORM: same size everywhere, hubs are invisible
nx.draw_networkx_edges(G, pos, ax=ax[0], edge_color=LINE, width=0.6)
nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G, pos, ax=ax[0], node_size=90,
                       node_color=BLUE, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=0.5)
ax[0].set_title("UNIFORM: HUBS HIDDEN", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# SIZE = CONNECTIONS: hubs grow and pop, top hubs in red
node_cols = [RED if d >= hub - 1 else BLUE for d in sizes]
nx.draw_networkx_edges(G, pos, ax=ax[1], edge_color=LINE, width=0.6)
nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G, pos, ax=ax[1], node_size=sizes * 45,
                       node_color=node_cols, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=0.5)
ax[1].set_title("SIZE = CONNECTIONS: HUBS POP", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.1)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python

                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G, pos, ax=ax[1], node_size=sizes * 45,
                       node_color=node_cols, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=0.5)
ax[1].set_title("SIZE = CONNECTIONS: HUBS POP", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.1)
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.takeaway}
Map size to a real quantity (degree, expression, effect size). Bigger reads as more, instantly.
:::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666;"}
After Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization* (2019), ch. 19.
:::


<!-- slide 12.2 -->
## Pre-attentive: Direction {.smaller}

[Honest charts · perception]{.eyebrow}

### Left vs right reads as down vs up

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
A volcano splits genes by the **sign** of the fold change: down-regulated to the left, up-regulated to the right. Position relative to zero *is* the direction, the eye sorts the two groups before reading a single label.

Like an age pyramid (male left, female right), direction carries meaning for free.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
np.random.seed(42)
n = 2000
log2fc = np.random.normal(0, 1.5, n)
pvals = np.random.exponential(0.4, n).clip(1e-30, 1)
# spike in 80 truly significant genes (40 up, 40 down)
sig_idx = np.random.choice(n, 80, replace=False)
log2fc[sig_idx[:40]] += 3
log2fc[sig_idx[40:]] -= 3
pvals[sig_idx] *= 1e-6
neg_log_p = -np.log10(pvals)

# split by DIRECTION: down-left (blue), up-right (red), rest grey
up = (log2fc > 1) & (neg_log_p > 1.3)
down = (log2fc < -1) & (neg_log_p > 1.3)
ns = ~(up | down)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.scatter(log2fc[ns], neg_log_p[ns], c=GREY, s=10, alpha=0.4, linewidths=0)
ax.scatter(log2fc[down], neg_log_p[down], c=BLUE, s=22, alpha=0.85, linewidths=0)
ax.scatter(log2fc[up], neg_log_p[up], c=RED, s=22, alpha=0.85, linewidths=0)
ax.axhline(1.3, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls="--")     # p = 0.05
ax.axvline(1, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls="--")       # 2-fold up
ax.axvline(-1, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls="--")      # 2-fold down
ax.text(-5.5, neg_log_p.max() * 0.92, f"DOWN {int(down.sum())}",
        color=BLUE, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(3, neg_log_p.max() * 0.92, f"UP {int(up.sum())}",
        color=RED, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("-log10 p", fontsize=8)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Code

<!-- slide 12.3 -->
## Pre-attentive: Direction with Bars {.smaller}

[Honest charts · perception]{.eyebrow}

### Anchor at zero, let the bars point up or down

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
The volcano shows direction by *position*; a diverging bar shows it by *length from zero*. Down-regulated genes grow left, up-regulated grow right, ranked by effect size.

Same pre-attentive idea as an age pyramid: one zero line, two directions, no legend needed.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
de = load_deseq2()                     # gene, log2FoldChange, pvalue, padj

# take the 8 most up- and 8 most down-regulated genes
top_up = de.nlargest(8, "log2FoldChange")
top_dn = de.nsmallest(8, "log2FoldChange")
sel = pd.concat([top_dn, top_up]).sort_values("log2FoldChange")
cols = [BLUE if v < 0 else RED for v in sel["log2FoldChange"]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.2))
ax.barh(range(len(sel)), sel["log2FoldChange"], color=cols, height=0.7)
ax.axvline(0, color=INK, lw=1.2)       # the zero divide = direction line
ax.set_yticks(range(len(sel)))
ax.set_yticklabels(sel["gene"], fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change", fontsize=9)
ax.text(-0.5, len(sel) - 0.5, "DOWN", color=BLUE,
        fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", ha="right")
ax.text(0.5, len(sel) - 0.5, "UP", color=RED,
        fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", ha="left")
ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 13 -->
# Colour in Data Visualization {.divider}

[Colour theory for charts · Day 01]{.eyebrow}

<!-- slide 14 -->
## Three Palette Types {.smaller}

[Colour · palette types]{.eyebrow}

### Match the palette to your data's structure

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="42%"}
**Qualitative** for unordered categories, **sequential** for magnitude (one hue, light to dark), **diverging** for signed values around zero (two hues, neutral midpoint).
::::

:::: {.column width="58%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-dpi: 200
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.6, 5))

# QUALITATIVE: distinct hues for unordered categories
cats = ["Liver", "Brain", "Heart", "Kidney", "Lung"]
cv = [72, 58, 85, 63, 91]
ax[0].barh(cats[::-1], cv[::-1],
           color=ECON_QUAL[:5][::-1], height=0.65)
ax[0].set_xlim(0, 105)
ax[0].set_title("QUALITATIVE", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax[0].tick_params(labelsize=7)
for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
    ax[0].spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax[0].xaxis.set_visible(False)

# SEQUENTIAL: one hue ramped light->dark for magnitude
sv = np.linspace(10, 90, 8)
cmap = econ_cmap("hongkong", reverse=True)
norm = plt.Normalize(0, 100)
ax[1].barh(range(8), sv,
           color=[cmap(norm(v)) for v in sv],
           height=0.7)
ax[1].set_yticks([])
ax[1].set_title("SEQUENTIAL", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
    ax[1].spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax[1].xaxis.set_visible(False)

# DIVERGING: two hues around a neutral 0 (down vs up)
genes = ["BRCA1", "TP53", "EGFR",
         "MYC", "KRAS", "PTEN"]
fc = [-2.1, -1.2, -0.3, 0.6, 1.4, 2.3]
norm = plt.Normalize(-3, 3)
ax[2].barh(genes, fc,
           color=[econ_diverging(norm(v)) for v in fc],
           height=0.65)
ax[2].axvline(0, color=LINE, lw=1)     # the neutral midpoint
ax[2].set_title("DIVERGING", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax[2].tick_params(labelsize=7)
for s in ["top", "right"]:
    ax[2].spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.55)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 15 -->
## The Rainbow Trap & Accessibility {.smaller}

[Colour · accessibility]{.eyebrow}

### Avoid rainbow scales, design for colour-blindness

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Hue has no natural order, so the brain cannot turn a rainbow back into magnitude. Prefer perceptually-uniform maps, avoid red-green pairs, and use the squint test.

About 5% of your audience is colour-blind.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-dpi: 200
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6, 5))
data = rng.normal(size=(12, 12))       # same data, two colourmaps

# JET: rainbow isn't ordered, it invents bands that aren't real
ax[0].imshow(data, cmap="jet", aspect="auto")
ax[0].set_title("JET (RAINBOW): MISLEADING",
                color=RED, fontsize=11,
                fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[0].set_xticks([])
ax[0].set_yticks([])

# VIRIDIS: perceptually uniform, equal steps look equal
ax[1].imshow(data, cmap="viridis", aspect="auto")
ax[1].set_title("VIRIDIS: UNIFORM", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[1].set_xticks([])
ax[1].set_yticks([])
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.3)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6, 5))
data = rng.normal(size=(12, 12))       # same data, two colourmaps

# JET: rainbow isn't ordered, it invents bands that aren't real
ax[0].imshow(data, cmap="jet", aspect="auto")
ax[0].set_title("JET (RAINBOW): MISLEADING",
                color=RED, fontsize=11,
                fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[0].set_xticks([])
ax[0].set_yticks([])

# VIRIDIS: perceptually uniform, equal steps look equal
ax[1].imshow(data, cmap="viridis", aspect="auto")
ax[1].set_title("VIRIDIS: UNIFORM", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[1].set_xticks([])
ax[1].set_yticks([])
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.3)
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666;"}
Crameri, Shephard & Heron (2020), *Nat. Commun.*
:::

<!-- slide 16.3 -->
## Colour Pitfall: Too Many Colours {.smaller}

[Colour · pitfalls]{.eyebrow}

### Don't give colour a job too big for it

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
One colour per gene across 30 genes is a rainbow with no meaning, the hues blur and the legend is useless. Group the genes into a few **pathways** and sort by group: now colour reads as six clean blocks instead of noise.

Keep categorical palettes to about 5 to 7 colours. Beyond that, group, facet, or label.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7.8
#| fig-height: 4
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
ngenes = 30
vals = rng.uniform(2, 10, ngenes)
pathway = rng.integers(0, 6, ngenes)            # each gene belongs to a pathway
names = ["Glycolysis", "TCA cycle", "Defense",
         "Hormone", "Cell wall", "Photosynth"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.8, 4))

# WRONG: one colour per gene -> 30 hues, meaningless
many = plt.get_cmap("hsv", ngenes)
ax[0].bar(range(ngenes), vals, color=[many(i) for i in range(ngenes)])
ax[0].set_title("ONE COLOUR PER GENE (30)", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax[0].set_ylabel("expression", fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_xticks([])

# RIGHT: sort by pathway so each colour forms one clean block
order = np.argsort(pathway)
ax[1].bar(range(ngenes), vals[order],
          color=[ECON_QUAL[p] for p in pathway[order]])
ax[1].set_title("GROUPED BY PATHWAY (6)", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax[1].set_xticks([])
for a in ax:
    a.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7)

# legend as one horizontal row BELOW both panels, off the bars
handles = [Patch(color=ECON_QUAL[p], label=names[p]) for p in range(6)]
fig.legend(handles=handles, fontsize=7, frameon=False,
           loc="lower center", ncol=6, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02))
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.2, bottom=0.16)
plt.show()
```

### Code


[The bottom line]{.tl}
When you have too many categories, group them. Colour by pathway, and sort so each group reads as a block.
:::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666;"}
After Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization* (2019), ch. 19.
:::

<!-- slide 16.4 -->
## Colour Pitfall: Colour for No Reason {.smaller}

[Colour · pitfalls]{.eyebrow}

### Don't encode in colour what's already shown

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
If the x-axis already tells you which tissue is which, colouring each bar a different hue adds nothing, it just adds visual load and a redundant legend. Use a single colour, and save a highlight hue for the one bar that matters.

Colour should add information, not decorate.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4
te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 4))

# WRONG: a different colour per bar, but the label already says which is which
ax[0].barh(te["tissue"], te["tpm"],
           color=ECON_QUAL[:len(te)], height=0.6)
ax[0].set_title("RAINBOW: COLOUR ADDS NOTHING", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# RIGHT: one colour, highlight only the bar that matters
bc = [GREEN if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te["tissue"]]
ax[1].barh(te["tissue"], te["tpm"], color=bc, height=0.6)
ax[1].set_title("ONE COLOUR + ONE HIGHLIGHT", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(0, 105); a.xaxis.set_visible(False)
    a.tick_params(labelsize=8)
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
        a.spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.4)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python
te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 4))

# WRONG: a different colour per bar, but the label already says which is which
ax[0].barh(te["tissue"], te["tpm"],
           color=ECON_QUAL[:len(te)], height=0.6)
ax[0].set_title("RAINBOW: COLOUR ADDS NOTHING", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# RIGHT: one colour, highlight only the bar that matters
bc = [GREEN if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te["tissue"]]
ax[1].barh(te["tissue"], te["tpm"], color=bc, height=0.6)
ax[1].set_title("ONE COLOUR + ONE HIGHLIGHT", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(0, 105); a.xaxis.set_visible(False)
    a.tick_params(labelsize=8)
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
        a.spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.4)
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.takeaway}
If the axis already identifies the category, colour is redundant. Spend it on the one thing you want seen.
:::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666;"}
After Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization* (2019), ch. 19.
:::

<!-- slide 16.5 -->
## Colour Pitfall: Forgetting Colour-Blindness {.smaller}

[Colour · pitfalls]{.eyebrow}

### Test your palette the way ~5% will see it

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="42%"}
A red/green pair looks fine to you and collapses to one colour for a red-green colour-blind reader. Always check under simulated deficiency, and pair colour with a second cue (shape, position, label).

These tools simulate it live, drop in your hexes and see.
::::

:::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.panel-tabset}

### viz-palette

```{=html}
<video controls loop muted width="100%" style="border-radius:8px;">
  <source src="images/vizalette.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
```

### pypalettes


::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
A red/green pair can vanish for ~5% of readers. Simulate it, and never let colour carry the message alone.

<!-- slide 16.6 -->
## Finding Good Palettes {.smaller}

[Colour · resources]{.eyebrow}

### Don't invent colours, borrow tested ones

Three rules for any palette: enough contrast, colour-blind safe, and only as many colours as you have groups. Rather than guessing hexes, pull from a curated source:

- **viz-palette** (`projects.susielu.com/viz-palette`), paste your hex list and simulate every type of colour-blindness.
- **R color palettes**, Emil Hvitfeldt (`emilhvitfeldt.github.io/r-color-palettes`), curated discrete sets (Wes Anderson, scientific) with copyable hex codes.
- **R Graph Gallery palette finder** (`r-graph-gallery.com/color-palette-finder`), browse and filter by palette type.

::: {.takeaway}
[In Python]{.tl}
`pypalettes` brings all these curated palettes into matplotlib: `load_cmap("Darjeeling1")` and you're done.
:::

<!-- slide 16.7 -->
## Typography for Scientific Figures {.smaller}

[Design · typography]{.eyebrow}

### Pick a font for the job, then stop choosing

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="42%"}
Five font categories, each with a job. For figures and slides you mostly need two: a clean **sans serif** for labels and a **monospace** for code and aligned numbers. A **display** face for titles is optional.

Pick one of each and reuse them everywhere, consistency reads as polish.

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:0.4em;"}
![](images/Ellen_Lumpton.png){width="32%"}

[Read]{.eyebrow} Ellen Lupton, *Thinking with Type*
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="58%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 3.4
rows = [
    ["Sans Serif", "Clean, modern", "Screen, slides", "Asap, Helvetica"],
    ["Serif", "Traditional, formal", "Papers, reports", "Georgia, Times"],
    ["Slab Serif", "Bold serifs, strong", "Headings, emphasis", "Rockwell, Courier"],
    ["Monospace", "Fixed-width", "Code, alignment", "JetBrains Mono"],
    ["Display", "Decorative, distinct", "Titles, branding", "Space Grotesk"],
]
cols = ["Category", "Characteristics", "Best used for", "Examples"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.4))
ax.axis("off")
tbl = ax.table(cellText=rows, colLabels=cols, cellLoc="left",
               loc="center", colWidths=[0.17, 0.28, 0.27, 0.28])
tbl.auto_set_font_size(False); tbl.set_fontsize(9); tbl.scale(1, 1.8)
for (r, c), cell in tbl.get_celld().items():
    cell.set_edgecolor(LINE)
    if r == 0:                                   # header row
        cell.set_text_props(weight="bold", color=INK)
        cell.set_facecolor(ECON["hongkong"][3])
    else:
        cell.set_facecolor(CREAM if r % 2 else "#FFFFFF")
        if c == 0:                               # category column
            cell.set_text_props(weight="bold", color=GREEN)
        else:
            cell.set_text_props(color=MUTED)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 16 -->
## Grey Is Your Best Friend {.smaller}

[Colour · strategic use]{.eyebrow}

### Highlight by de-emphasising everything else

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Grey the 95% that is context, colour the 5% that matters. In a volcano of 2,000 genes, the significant hits should be the only thing in colour.

Like silence in music, it makes the melody stand out.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.1
#| fig-dpi: 200
np.random.seed(42)
n = 2000
log2fc = np.random.normal(0, 1.5, n)
pvals = np.random.exponential(0.4, n).clip(1e-30, 1)
# spike in 80 truly significant genes so the arms are dense
sig_idx = np.random.choice(n, 80, replace=False)
log2fc[sig_idx[:40]] += 3
log2fc[sig_idx[40:]] -= 3
pvals[sig_idx] *= 1e-6
neg_log_p = -np.log10(pvals)

# significant = big fold change AND small p-value
sig = (np.abs(log2fc) > 1) & (neg_log_p > 1.3)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.6))

# CONTEXT: grey the 95%, faint and small so it recedes
ax.scatter(log2fc[~sig], neg_log_p[~sig],
           c=GREY, s=8, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
# MESSAGE: colour the 5% that matters, bigger and bolder
ax.scatter(log2fc[sig], neg_log_p[sig],
           c=RED, s=20, alpha=0.85,
           edgecolors=CREAM, lw=0.3)
ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change")
ax.set_ylabel("-log10 p")
ax.set_title("GREY + ONE HIGHLIGHT", color=GREEN,
             fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 17 -->
# From Chart to Story {.divider}

[Narrative data visualization · Day 01]{.eyebrow}

<!-- slide 19 -->
## The Story Arc {.smaller}

[Storytelling · arc]{.eyebrow}

### Every data presentation needs tension and resolution

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
A single figure rarely tells the whole story. Open with context, raise a challenge (which loci?), show the action (fine-mapping), then resolve it with the causal variant. Chapters, not one slide.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-dpi: 200
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.7))

# a rising-then-resting curve = engagement over the talk
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
y = 0.5 + 4 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - 5.5) / 2.2) ** 2)
ax.fill_between(x, 0, y, color=GREEN, alpha=0.15)
ax.plot(x, y, color=GREEN, lw=3)

# mark the four story beats along the curve
for xp, lab in [(1.2, "OPENING"), (3.5, "CHALLENGE"),
                (5.5, "CLIMAX"), (7.7, "RESOLUTION")]:
    yp = 0.5 + 4 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((xp - 5.5) / 2.2) ** 2)
    ax.plot(xp, yp, "o", color=GREEN, markersize=10, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(lab, (xp, yp), textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=(0, 14), ha="center", fontsize=8,
                fontweight="bold", color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("presentation flow")
ax.set_ylabel("engagement")
ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 6.2)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title("THE STORY ARC", color="#333333",
             fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 21 -->
## Build Up Towards Complexity {.smaller}

[Storytelling · progressive disclosure]{.eyebrow}

### Show a simple version first, then reveal the full picture

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Teach the reader to read **one** panel first, then show the full grid with shared scales. Like playing one bar on the piano before handing over the orchestral score.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-dpi: 200
tc = load_timecourse()                 # gene, time, tpm, sem
piv = tc.pivot(index="time", columns="gene", values="tpm")
genes = list(piv.columns)
tp = np.arange(len(piv.index))
tl = [f"{t}h" for t in piv.index]

# one panel per gene, shared scales so they compare
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(6.4, 4.7),
                       sharex=True, sharey=True)
for a, g in zip(ax.flat, genes):
    a.plot(tp, piv[g].values, "-o", color=GREEN,
           lw=1.8, markersize=4)
    a.set_title(g, fontsize=9, fontweight="bold",
                color="#333333")
    a.set_xticks(tp); a.set_xticklabels(tl, fontsize=6)
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=6)
fig.suptitle("ONE GENE, THEN THE GRID",
             color="#333333", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.4, wspace=0.2, top=0.86)
plt.show()
```

## Editorial Thinking: Angle, Frame, Focus {.smaller}

[Storytelling · editorial]{.eyebrow}

### Put the finding in the title, the highlight on one bar

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
"Expression varies across tissues" is a topic. "Heart shows the highest BRCA1" is an **angle**, so put it in the title. Frame to the tissues that matter, focus with one highlight colour.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-dpi: 200
te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 4.7))

# TOPIC: no angle, all one grey, title just names the axes
ax[0].barh(te["tissue"], te["tpm"], color=GREY, height=0.5)
ax[0].set_title("EXPRESSION ACROSS TISSUES",
                color="#333333", fontsize=10,
                fontweight="bold", pad=6)

# ANGLE: finding in the title, one bar highlighted
bc = [GREEN if t == "Heart" else GREY
      for t in te["tissue"]]
ax[1].barh(te["tissue"], te["tpm"], color=bc, height=0.5)
ax[1].set_title("HEART SHOWS HIGHEST BRCA1",
                color=GREEN, fontsize=10,
                fontweight="bold", pad=6)
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(0, 105); a.xaxis.set_visible(False)
    a.tick_params(labelsize=8)
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
        a.spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.5)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 20 -->
## Make a Figure for the Generals {.smaller}

[Storytelling · simplicity]{.eyebrow}

### If a busy reader can't get the point in ten seconds, simplify

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
The generals aren't slow, they're busy. If five data dimensions are tangential to your point, strip them down to the one comparison that answers the question. *(after Claus Wilke)*
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-dpi: 200
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.7))

# TOO COMPLEX: colour, size, and scatter all at once
n = 130
tis = rng.choice(["Brain", "Liver", "Heart",
                  "Kidney", "Lung"], n)
x = rng.normal(50, 15, n)
y = 0.3 * x + rng.normal(0, 8, n)
s = rng.uniform(20, 200, n)
tc = dict(zip(["Brain", "Liver", "Heart",
               "Kidney", "Lung"], ECON_QUAL[:5]))
ax[0].scatter(x, y, c=[tc[t] for t in tis], s=s,
              alpha=0.5, edgecolors=CREAM, lw=0.3)
ax[0].set_title("TOO COMPLEX", color=RED,
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[0].set_xlabel("feature A", fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_ylabel("feature B", fontsize=8)

# ONE CLEAR MESSAGE: rank the tissues, highlight the winner
te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")
bc = [GREEN if t == "Heart" else GREY
      for t in te["tissue"]]
ax[1].barh(te["tissue"], te["tpm"], color=bc, height=0.6)
ax[1].set_title("ONE CLEAR MESSAGE", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[1].set_xlim(0, 105)
for sp in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
    ax[1].spines[sp].set_visible(False)
ax[1].xaxis.set_visible(False)
ax[1].tick_params(labelsize=8)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.45, bottom=0.16)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 22 -->
## Memorability vs Minimalism {.smaller}

[Storytelling · memorability]{.eyebrow}

### Simple is clear, distinctive is remembered

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Tufte says strip everything, research says distinctive figures stick. Both are right: add elements that **carry meaning**, one consistent colour per assay and the key number, never decoration.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-dpi: 200
ac = load_assay_counts()               # assay, n_datasets
m = ac["assay"].tolist()
c = ac["n_datasets"].tolist()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 4.7))

# PLAIN: all grey, nothing to anchor the memory
ax[0].barh(m[::-1], c[::-1], color=GREY, height=0.55)
for i, v in enumerate(c[::-1]):
    ax[0].text(v + 5, i, str(v), va="center",
               fontsize=9, color=MUTED)
ax[0].set_title("PLAIN: FORGETTABLE", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[0].set_xlim(0, 400)

# SEMANTIC: one colour per assay + the number = sticky
cols = [GREEN, BLUE, PURPLE, RED]
ax[1].barh(m[::-1], c[::-1], color=cols[::-1], height=0.55)
for i, (v, col) in enumerate(zip(c[::-1], cols[::-1])):
    ax[1].text(v + 5, i, f"{v} datasets", va="center",
               fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=col)
ax[1].set_title("SEMANTIC: MEMORABLE", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[1].set_xlim(0, 470)

# curved annotation: point at the standout RNA-seq bar
ax[1].annotate("the one\nyou remember",
               xy=(345, 2.75), xytext=(360, 1.3),
               fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=GREEN,
               va="center", ha="left",
               arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GREEN, lw=1.6,
                               connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.4"))

for a in ax:
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
        a.spines[s].set_visible(False)
    a.xaxis.set_visible(False); a.tick_params(labelsize=8)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.5)
plt.show()
```

```python
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[0].set_xlim(0, 400)

# SEMANTIC: one colour per assay + the number = sticky
cols = [GREEN, BLUE, PURPLE, RED]
ax[1].barh(m[::-1], c[::-1], color=cols[::-1], height=0.55)
for i, (v, col) in enumerate(zip(c[::-1], cols[::-1])):
    ax[1].text(v + 5, i, f"{v} datasets", va="center",
               fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=col)
ax[1].set_title("SEMANTIC: MEMORABLE", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[1].set_xlim(0, 470)

# curved annotation: point at the standout RNA-seq bar
ax[1].annotate("the one\nyou remember",
               xy=(345, 2.75), xytext=(360, 1.3),
               fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=GREEN,
               va="center", ha="left",
               arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GREEN, lw=1.6,
                               connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.4"))

for a in ax:
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
        a.spines[s].set_visible(False)
    a.xaxis.set_visible(False); a.tick_params(labelsize=8)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.5)
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666;"}
Bateman et al. (2010), *ACM CHI*.
:::

<!-- slide 16.1 -->
## Data Transformations {.smaller}

[Honest charts · scales]{.eyebrow}

### Log the axis when values span orders of magnitude

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Expression, counts, and p-values are **right-skewed**: most values are small, a few are huge. On a linear axis everything crushes left. A log axis spreads them out and the real shape appears.

Log for orders of magnitude, sqrt for counts, linear for a narrow range.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-dpi: 200
vals = 10 ** rng.normal(1.2, 0.8, 2000)   # right-skewed expression
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 4))

# LINEAR: a few huge values crush everything to the left
ax[0].hist(vals, bins=40, color=GREY)
ax[0].set_title("LINEAR: crushed", color=RED,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[0].set_xlabel("expression (TPM)")

# LOG: log-spaced bins + log axis reveal the bell shape
bins = np.logspace(np.log10(vals.min()),
                   np.log10(vals.max()), 40)
ax[1].hist(vals, bins=bins, color=GREEN)
ax[1].set_xscale("log")
ax[1].set_title("LOG: shape visible", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[1].set_xlabel("expression (TPM, log)")
for a in ax:
    a.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    a.set_yticks([])
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.25, bottom=0.16)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python
vals = 10 ** rng.normal(1.2, 0.8, 2000)   # right-skewed expression
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 4))

# LINEAR: a few huge values crush everything to the left
ax[0].hist(vals, bins=40, color=GREY)
ax[0].set_title("LINEAR: crushed", color=RED,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[0].set_xlabel("expression (TPM)")

# LOG: log-spaced bins + log axis reveal the bell shape
bins = np.logspace(np.log10(vals.min()),
                   np.log10(vals.max()), 40)
ax[1].hist(vals, bins=bins, color=GREEN)
ax[1].set_xscale("log")
ax[1].set_title("LOG: shape visible", color=GREEN,
                fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax[1].set_xlabel("expression (TPM, log)")
for a in ax:
    a.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    a.set_yticks([])
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.25, bottom=0.16)
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.takeaway}
Log for data spanning orders of magnitude, sqrt for counts, linear for a narrow range. Always label the axis as transformed.
:::

<!-- slide 16.2 -->
## Seeing Through Overplotting {.smaller}

[Honest charts · density]{.eyebrow}

### When points pile up, reveal the density

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="42%"}
Thousands of solid points become one blob. Four fixes: **transparency** (alpha) plus a thin edge, **jitter** to separate stacked points, and a **density contour** to show where the mass actually is.
::::

:::: {.column width="58%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-dpi: 200
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
n = 1500                                   # two overlapping clouds
x = np.concatenate([rng.normal(3, 0.8, n),
                    rng.normal(6, 0.7, n // 2)])
y = np.concatenate([rng.normal(20, 4, n)
                    - 2 * rng.normal(3, 0.8, n),
                    rng.normal(12, 2, n // 2)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7.6, 6))

# NAIVE: solid opaque points merge into a blob
ax[0, 0].scatter(x, y, color=BLUE, s=20)
ax[0, 0].set_title("NAIVE: solid points", color=RED,
                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# ALPHA + thin edge: transparency shows density
ax[0, 1].scatter(x, y, color=BLUE, s=20, alpha=0.18,
                 edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=0.3)
ax[0, 1].set_title("ALPHA + edge", color="#333333",
                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# JITTER: nudge each point so stacked ones spread
jx = x + rng.normal(0, 0.12, len(x))
jy = y + rng.normal(0, 0.4, len(y))
ax[1, 0].scatter(jx, jy, color=BLUE, s=14,
                 alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none")
ax[1, 0].set_title("JITTER", color="#333333",
                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# DENSITY CONTOUR: KDE shows where the mass actually is
kde = gaussian_kde(np.vstack([x, y]))
xg, yg = np.mgrid[x.min():x.max():80j,
                  y.min():y.max():80j]
zz = kde(np.vstack([xg.ravel(),
                    yg.ravel()])).reshape(xg.shape)
ax[1, 1].scatter(x, y, color=GREY, s=6,
                 alpha=0.15, edgecolors="none")
ax[1, 1].contour(xg, yg, zz, levels=6,
                 cmap="viridis", linewidths=1.2)
ax[1, 1].set_title("DENSITY CONTOUR", color="#333333",
                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
for a in ax.flat:
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    a.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.15, hspace=0.3)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python
                    yg.ravel()])).reshape(xg.shape)
ax[1, 1].scatter(x, y, color=GREY, s=6,
                 alpha=0.15, edgecolors="none")
ax[1, 1].contour(xg, yg, zz, levels=6,
                 cmap="viridis", linewidths=1.2)

                   fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
for a in ax.flat:

    a.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.15, hspace=0.3)
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Solid points hide structure. Add transparency and a thin edge, jitter to unstack, or draw a density contour to show where points concentrate.
:::

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.58em; color: #666666;"}
After Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization* (2019), ch. 18.
:::




<!-- slide 23 -->
## Don't Repeat Yourself: Vary Chart Types {.smaller}

[Storytelling · variety]{.eyebrow}

### Use a different visualization for each distinct analysis

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Two bar charts blur together. Use a **bar** for the discrete comparison and a **line** for the time course, and each panel reads as its own idea.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-dpi: 200
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.6))

# COMPARISON: discrete conditions -> bar
cond = ["Control", "Drug A", "Drug B"]; ev = [45, 68, 72]
ax[0].barh(cond[::-1], ev[::-1],
           color=[BLUE, BLUE, GREY][::-1], height=0.55)
for i, v in enumerate(ev[::-1]):
    ax[0].text(v + 1, i, str(v), va="center",
               fontsize=9, color=MUTED)
ax[0].set_title("COMPARISON (BAR)", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[0].set_xlim(0, 85)
for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]:
    ax[0].spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax[0].xaxis.set_visible(False); ax[0].tick_params(labelsize=8)

# TIME COURSE: continuous time -> line
tm = ["0h", "6h", "12h", "24h"]; tv = [45, 55, 68, 72]
ax[1].plot(tm, tv, "-o", color=GREEN, lw=2.5, markersize=8)
ax[1].fill_between(range(4), [v - 4 for v in tv],
                   [v + 4 for v in tv], color=GREEN, alpha=0.12)
ax[1].set_title("TIME COURSE (LINE)", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[1].tick_params(labelsize=8)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.35)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python

ax[1].plot(tm, tv, "-o", color=GREEN, lw=2.5, markersize=8)
ax[1].fill_between(range(4), [v - 4 for v in tv],
                   [v + 4 for v in tv], color=GREEN, alpha=0.12)
ax[1].set_title("TIME COURSE (LINE)", color="#333333",
                fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", pad=6)
ax[1].tick_params(labelsize=8)
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.35)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 24 -->
## Small Multiples · Step 1: the spaghetti problem {.smaller}

[Storytelling · faceting]{.eyebrow}

### Six genes on one axis overlap into an unreadable tangle

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Plotting many series on a single axis quickly becomes spaghetti: the lines cross, the legend grows, and no one trend is followable.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-dpi: 200
tc = load_timecourse()                 # gene, time, tpm, sem
piv = tc.pivot(index="time", columns="gene", values="tpm")
genes = list(piv.columns)
tp = np.arange(len(piv.index))
tl = [f"{t}h" for t in piv.index]

# all six genes on ONE axis = tangled spaghetti
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.7))
for g, c in zip(genes, ECON_QUAL[:6]):
    ax.plot(tp, piv[g].values, "-o", color=c,
            lw=2.2, markersize=5, label=g, alpha=0.8)
ax.set_xticks(tp); ax.set_xticklabels(tl)
ax.set_ylabel("Expression (TPM)")
ax.set_title("SPAGHETTI: HARD TO FOLLOW", color=RED,
             fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", pad=8)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, ncol=3, loc="upper left")
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 25 -->
## Small Multiples · Step 2: the faceted fix {.smaller}

[Storytelling · faceting]{.eyebrow}

### One small panel per gene, with shared scales, scans at a glance

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="44%"}
Give each series its own panel and **share the axes** so the panels are comparable. The eye scans a grid far faster than it untangles overlapping lines.
::::

:::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-dpi: 200
tc = load_timecourse()                 # gene, time, tpm, sem
piv = tc.pivot(index="time", columns="gene", values="tpm")
genes = list(piv.columns)
tp = np.arange(len(piv.index))
tl = [f"{t}h" for t in piv.index]

# one panel per gene, sharex/sharey so they compare
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(6.6, 4.7),
                       sharex=True, sharey=True)
for a, (g, c) in zip(ax.flat, zip(genes, ECON_QUAL[:6])):
    a.plot(tp, piv[g].values, "-o", color=c,
           lw=2.2, markersize=5)
    a.set_title(g, fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=c)
    a.set_xticks(tp); a.set_xticklabels(tl, fontsize=6)
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=6)
fig.suptitle("SMALL MULTIPLES: EASY TO SCAN",
             color="#333333", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.4, wspace=0.2, top=0.86)
plt.show()
```

### Code

```python
tc = load_timecourse()                 # gene, time, tpm, sem
piv = tc.pivot(index="time", columns="gene", values="tpm")
genes = list(piv.columns)
tp = np.arange(len(piv.index))
tl = [f"{t}h" for t in piv.index]

# one panel per gene, sharex/sharey so they compare
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(6.6, 4.7),
                       sharex=True, sharey=True)
for a, (g, c) in zip(ax.flat, zip(genes, ECON_QUAL[:6])):
    a.plot(tp, piv[g].values, "-o", color=c,
           lw=2.2, markersize=5)
    a.set_title(g, fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=c)
    a.set_xticks(tp); a.set_xticklabels(tl, fontsize=6)
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=6)
fig.suptitle("SMALL MULTIPLES: EASY TO SCAN",
             color="#333333", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.4, wspace=0.2, top=0.86)
plt.show()
```
